To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Android's design is based on the sharing of public resources, which is a potential source of serious privacy breaches; 2) We discovered three unexpected and previously unstudied channels of information leaks; 3) We show that an app without any permissions may acquire sensitive information from top-of-the line Android apps; and 4) We propose a mitigation mechanism to achieve a delicate balance between the utility and privacy of these resources.
Android public resources can be exploited to leak sensitive information and the proposed mitigation mechanism can effectively prevent such information leaks.

(a) Android public resources are not as safe as they are assumed to be; (b) an app can be used to infer sensitive information from public background information; (c) an app can also be abused to determine the running status of another app; (d) we propose a mitigation mechanism that can achieve a good trade-off between utility and privacy
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions. Can an adversary infer sensitive information from the public shared resources of an Android device? If so, what is the scope of such privacy breaches? How can we mitigate the privacy threats without compromising the functionality of these resources?

a fundamental question: can an app with no permission infer sensitive information of its user? We believe this question is of great significance in Android security, and our findings and mitigation mechanism will help improve the security of the Android ecosystem.

three aspects: (1) the discovery of information leaks from public resources; (2) the design and implementation of a novel zero-permission app that can collect sensitive information from public resources and stealthily send it to a remote attacker, and (3) the design of a mitigation mechanism to address the information leaks from public shared resources.
